newsitem.title: UK: Sea Empress oil spill report small print could cost.
newsitem.headline: Sea Empress oil spill report small print could cost.

text.p: A little-noticed recommendation in the official report into Britain's Sea Empress grounding threatens to involve heavy costs for the tanker industry, sources across the shipping world have said.
It may also once again inflame relations between tanker owners and regulators over measures aimed at protecting the environment from oil spills.

The U.K. government report into the 71,800 tonne oil spill which followed the February 1996 grounding of the suezmax tanker off the south Wales port of Milford Haven primarily blamed pilot error and recommended improvements to training.

But the Marine Accident Investigation Branch (MAIB) report also proposed that regulations be amended to require tankers to have double bottoms under their pump rooms. It did so because use of the pumps was lost during the incident.

After the grounding, the Sea Empress was repaired by Northern Ireland shipyard Harland & Wolff to her original single hull configuration at a cost of $30 million. It did not involve fitting a double skin to the pump room.

H&W ship repair company managing director Jim Eccles said that a rough estimate for the extra cost of adding a double bottom to the pump room of the Sea Empress would have been in the region of $800,000.

The United Nation's International Maritime Organisation (IMO) has introduced regulations to phase out the use of single hull vessels by the year 2026 while requiring new tankers to be built with double hulls around thier cargo tanks - but with no specification for pump rooms.
An IMO spokesman said the organisation would put any recommendations on tanker design from the U.K. to its members.
He said it would be up to governments' representatives to decide whether any further changes were necessary - possibly along the lines of introducing already planned changes earlier.

"But you cannot keep changing the regulations every time there is an accident and you cannot alter ships over night," he said. "A lot of work has already be done and it is a matter of putting existing measures into effect."
Tanker owners fought in vain against U.S. proposals for mandatory double hulls in the aftermath of the oil spill from the Exxon Valdez in 1989, arguing they were unproven and costly.

The MAIB report asks Britain to encourage the revision by the IMO of marine pollution (Marpol) regulations: "To include the requirement that every oil tanker of 5,000 tonnes deadweight and above shall be fitted with a double bottom over the area of the pump room."
The work would involve moving pumps and their pipework higher and retro-fitting a second floor.
Many shipping industry insiders have expressed suprised at the recommendation which on the surface appears to have little connection with the loss of oil from the Sea Empress.
Independent oil tanker owners' organisation Intertanko argues that retro-fitting of double bottoms to tankers is technically feasible but not economically so.

Intertanko technical manager Dragos Rauta said earlier studies into the economic feasibility of fitting double hulls to older single skinned tankers had highlighted not only the cost but a lack of shipyard capacity to cope with the work.
Rauta said studies had also shown that most ships grounded bow first and that was where damage usually occcured. The benefits of protecting a pump room at the aft of the vessel were dubious, he said.
But there are technical difficulties too.
Eccles said pumps are located at the lowest point in the vessel to give them the suction to empty oil from right down in the bottom of cargo tanks. Lifting them up would reduce this ability.

Eccles said the advantage in protecting the pump room lay in retaining the ability of the ship's own equipment to remove oil from its tanks. Onboard pumps are up to four times faster than mobile equipment operated from a vessel brought alongside to remove oil before it spilled.

However, the MAIB report makes clear that most of the environmental damage from the Sea Empress occurred because the ship was not moved quickly after its first grounding. Only about 2,500 tonnes of oil were lost in the initial grounding, it said.
The report also maintains that oil pollution would probably have been avoided in the initial grounding if the ship had been built with a double hull.
Intertanko does not oppose the use of double hulls but claims that differing casualty conditions will determine whether they are a benefit or hindrance.
The Department of Transport says it will issue details of its findings following a six week consultation period that closes around the end of August.
